challenges.situation: A freelancer has built a strong reputation over 5 years. A client offers triple their normal rate for a project that requires cutting corners on quality — no one would notice. The project is a one-off with no future work expected. What does reputation math say?

options.text: Still don't cut corners — the client's network talks, and one negative data point propagates faster than five years of positive ones. The 'one-off' frame is usually wrong.
options.feedback: Reputation math says: one-offs are rarely truly one-off. The client's network overlaps with yours. One negative signal propagates exponentially while positive ones propagate linearly. The 'triple rate' is finite; the reputation damage is potentially unbounded. NDAs (option D) don't prevent word-of-mouth. Middle ground (option C) still compromises the standard your reputation is built on.

options.text: Take it — this is a one-shot game and reputation only matters in repeated interactions
options.feedback: Not quite. Reputation math says: one-offs are rarely truly one-off. The client's network overlaps with yours.

options.text: Negotiate a middle ground — do slightly less quality for a moderate premium
options.feedback: Not quite. Reputation math says: one-offs are rarely truly one-off. The client's network overlaps with yours.

options.text: Take it but ensure the contract prevents the client from sharing negative reviews

challenges.situation: The Medici bank charged LOWER interest rates than competitors — yet attracted FAR more deposits and became the dominant bank in Europe.
challenges.question: What force made 'cheaper' more profitable?

options.text: Trust — their century of never-default reputation made depositors feel safe, attracting massive volume that compensated for lower margins
options.feedback: The Medici's competitive advantage was trust: depositors chose safety over higher returns. This produced volume that exceeded what higher-margin competitors could attract. It's the trust premium — reputation as a moat. Status (B) was an effect, not the cause. They didn't limit deposits (C). And lower lending rates (D) would reduce profits; the advantage was on the deposit side — people giving them money to hold.

options.text: Status — being the pope's bank attracted clients who wanted the prestige of banking with the Medici
options.feedback: Not quite. The Medici's competitive advantage was trust: depositors chose safety over higher returns. This produced volume that exceeded what higher-margin competitors could attract.

options.text: Scarcity — they limited who could deposit, creating exclusivity that attracted more demand
options.feedback: Not quite. The Medici's competitive advantage was trust: depositors chose safety over higher returns. This produced volume that exceeded what higher-margin competitors could attract.

options.text: Incentives — their lower rates incentivized borrowers to choose them over competitors

challenges.instruction: Match each concept to its description:

items.text: Medici never defaulting even when they could → Protecting reputation's compound returns over any single-transaction profit
Enron winning 'Most Innovative' for 6 years then collapsing → Reputation built on false signals — exponential destruction when truth emerged
Arthur Andersen dissolving after Enron association → Reputation contagion — proximity to one bad actor destroyed a century-old firm
J&J immediately recalling Tylenol in 1982 → Rapid transparent repair that preserved (and enhanced) long-term reputation
A freelancer always delivering one day early → Small consistent data points compounding into 'reliable' faster than any grand gesture

challenges.context: Which response shows better understanding of the underlying dynamics?

scenarioA.label: Transaction-by-transaction thinking
scenarioA.text: Each deal is separate. I'll optimize each interaction for maximum return. If I can get away with something, the rational move is to take the gain while the cost is low.

scenarioB.label: Reputation-as-portfolio thinking
scenarioB.text: Every interaction is a data point in my permanent record. I protect my reputation's compound returns above any single transaction's gain — because the math always favors long-term trust over short-term extraction in repeated games.

challenges.explanation: The second response shows structural awareness — recognizing the game and changing it, rather than just playing harder within the existing frame.

principle.text: Reputation in repeated games is compound interest in trust. Each honest action earns a return that reinvests — making future honest actions more credible and attracting more opportunity.
principle.subtext: Reputation is asymmetric: it builds slowly (linear) and destroys instantly (exponential). This asymmetry means that protecting reputation should dominate almost every short-term optimization.

reflection: If someone investigated your last five decisions, would they find a consistent pattern — or would they see someone optimizing for short-term gains at reputation's expense?
